title: Sales + Solutions Engineering Training Notes — Enterprise Security Enablement Kit Rollout (2026)
body:
Audience
- AEs, SEs, CS (enterprise), Deal Desk partners who get pulled into late-stage security/compliance.

Goal of this training
- Make it easy to answer 80% of security/compliance questions with a consistent, approved narrative.
- Reduce “backchannel” answers in email/Slack that drift from approved claims.
- Shorten time-to-response for SOC 2 and evidence requests without violating access controls.

What is the Enterprise Security Enablement Kit (and what it is not)
- It is a curated set of customer-facing artifacts (FAQ + one-pagers + RFP response blocks) plus an internal process for evidence requests and exceptions.
- It is not a promise of roadmap items, future certifications, or custom control implementations.
- If a customer asks for “confirmation” outside the approved language, treat it as an exception and follow the escalation path below.

Where the kit lives (single source of truth)
- Canonical landing page (bookmark this): Confluence → Sales Enablement → “Enterprise Security Enablement Kit — Index”.
- Use Confluence as the source of truth for any language that will be pasted into:
  - RFP responses
  - security questionnaires
  - security addenda
  - procurement emails
- Google Drive drafts are working docs only. Do not send Drive drafts to customers unless Security/GRC explicitly approves.

What changed in the 2026 refresh (talk track)
1) Clear deployment-mode boundaries (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- We now explicitly differentiate controls and responsibilities by deployment mode.
- Hosted: Redwood-managed infrastructure + Redwood-managed runtime and control plane.
- Dedicated: isolated capacity + stronger data separation posture; still Redwood-managed ops unless otherwise contracted.
- Private (VPC/on-prem options): customer-controlled networking boundary; additional key management and logging options; shared responsibility model is more explicit.

2) Tightened data retention + deletion language
- Removed ambiguous phrases like “we don’t store data” without qualifiers.
- Added clearer definitions: request payload retention, generated outputs, application logs, and audit logs.
- Added “what you can configure” vs “what is fixed by deployment mode.”

3) Standard answers for SSO/SCIM/RBAC and audit logs are now copy/paste ready
- We have a standardized block for:
  - SSO/SAML (supported patterns)
  - SCIM provisioning (availability + scope)
  - RBAC model (roles/permissions, console/API coverage)
  - Audit log event types + export options (where supported)

4) Versioning discipline (important for RFPs)
- Security FAQ now has a clear version/date and a change log.
- Sales should cite the version/date in RFPs and questionnaires when pasting from the FAQ or library.
- If a customer asks “is this still accurate?”, point to the “Last reviewed” date and offer the evidence request process where applicable.

5) Stronger “what we do and don’t say” guardrails
- ISO language: alignment vs certification (do not imply certification unless explicitly approved).
- Pen test wording: do not quote frequency or scope beyond approved statement; do not share reports without the evidence process.
- Data residency: avoid blanket promises; use region-specific approved phrasing.

How to use the kit in real deals (recommended workflow)
Step 1 — Identify the deal motion
- Lightweight questionnaire (10–30 questions) → Use Security FAQ + standard answer blocks.
- Full RFP / security addendum → Use RFP response library blocks; cite version/date; route any contractual language to Legal.
- Regulated workload / Private deployment → Pull in SE lead + regulated deployments SME early; do not rely on Hosted-only statements.

Step 2 — Start with the customer’s top 3 blockers
Common top blockers we’ve seen:
- “Do you train on our data?”
- “Can we control retention/deletion?”
- “Do you support SSO/SCIM and audit log export to our SIEM?”
- “EU data residency requirements”
- “SOC 2 report under NDA”

Step 3 — Send the minimal set of artifacts
- Default package to send (unless they ask for more):
  - Enterprise Security FAQ (customer-facing)
  - Relevant one-pager(s): SOC 2 posture, data residency/retention, encryption/KMS, audit logging, SSO/RBAC
- For SOC 2 report: do not attach the report directly. Use the evidence request process.

Step 4 — Log what you sent + follow-up action
- Put the exact kit version/date in HubSpot notes and in the email thread.
- If you used a non-standard answer, open an exception request (see escalation).

Copy/paste “email wrapper” you can use
Subject: Redwood Inference — Security & Compliance Materials

Hi <Name>,

Sharing our current Enterprise Security Enablement materials for your review:
- Enterprise Security FAQ (Last reviewed: <date>; Version: <v>)
- <One-pager(s) relevant to their questions>

For SOC 2 report and certain evidence artifacts, we provide those under NDA via our evidence request process. If helpful, please share your due date and the list of requested items and we’ll coordinate.

Best,
<Name>

Common pitfalls (please avoid)
1) Over-claiming certifications
- Do not say “ISO 27001 certified” unless explicitly approved by GRC for that timeframe and entity.
- Use the approved “alignment” language where provided.

2) Over-simplifying data handling
- Avoid: “We never store prompts” or “No logs.”
- Use: “Data handling depends on deployment mode and customer configuration; see the retention/deletion overview.”
- If pressed, escalate; do not improvise exact retention windows.

3) Data residency blanket statements
- Avoid: “All data stays in the EU” without verifying:
  - which region(s) are in scope
  - which deployment mode
  - what logs/telemetry are included
- Use the EMEA-approved phrasing. If the customer requires contractual residency guarantees, route to Legal + GRC.

4) Pen test report / vuln scan details via email
- Do not forward reports or screenshots from restricted evidence folders.
- Use the evidence request playbook; confirm NDA status.

5) “Roadmap leakage”
- If a customer asks for a missing control (“Can you do X?”):
  - Answer only current capabilities.
  - Offer acceptable alternatives (from the exceptions policy).
  - If needed, ask Product Security PM to confirm whether it is supported today.

6) Confusing audit logs vs application logs
- Audit logs: security-relevant and admin/control-plane events.
- Application logs: service logs, request/response metadata (handling varies by deployment and config).
- Use the audit logging overview doc definitions.

High-frequency Q&A quick guidance (when to use which artifact)
A) “Do you train on customer data?”
- Use Security FAQ section on data use/training definitions.
- Key nuance: clarify what counts as “training,” what is excluded, and what controls apply to support/troubleshooting access.
- If customer asks for contract language: route to Legal; do not draft.

B) “What is your data retention policy? Can we set retention to 0?”
- Use retention/deletion overview + data residency/retention one-pager.
- If they require a hard guarantee of 0-day retention across all logs: treat as an exception; loop in Security/GRC and SE.

C) “Do you support SSO/SAML and SCIM?”
- Use standard answers doc + authoritative SSO/SAML/SCIM/RBAC capabilities page.
- Confirm whether they need:
  - SSO only (most common)
  - SCIM provisioning (who/what resources)
  - RBAC granularity requirements (admin vs viewer vs billing)

D) “Do you have audit logs and can we export to our SIEM?”
- Use audit logging overview + standard answer block.
- Confirm target: Splunk/Datadog/S3/SIEM pipeline.
- If the customer needs a specific schema/field, use the approved event taxonomy language; do not invent fields.

E) “Encryption at rest / in transit / KMS / HSM?”
- Use encryption + KMS one-pager.
- Be explicit about shared responsibility and boundaries by deployment mode.
- If they ask for customer-managed keys in a specific environment, confirm availability for their deployment mode; if unclear, escalate to Security Eng + SE.

F) “Subprocessors list / DPA?”
- Use the canonical link from the kit index.
- Route DPA redlines to Legal (Michael Grant) and log in the deal record.

Handling RFPs and questionnaires (process)
- Always paste from approved sources:
  - RFP response library blocks
  - Security FAQ standard language
- Include the version/date in your RFP response footer or internal notes.
- If you must deviate:
  - mark the deviation clearly
  - request approval before sending

Evidence requests (SOC 2 report, pen test attestation, policies)
- Use the SOC 2 customer evidence request playbook.
- Rules of thumb:
  - SOC 2 report is shared under NDA only.
  - Only GRC-approved responders (or designees) send restricted artifacts.
  - Set expectations early on timeline and NDA requirement to avoid last-minute escalations.

Escalation matrix (who to ping, and when)
1) “Is this control supported today?” / product capability ambiguity
- Primary: Markus Klein (SE lead)
- For Private/deployment specifics: Colin O’Donnell (Private deployment SME) or Fatima Noor (regulated deployments SME)
- For roadmap alignment / do-not-say: Naomi Feldman (Product Security PM)

2) Compliance language, audits, evidence, certifications
- Primary: Olga Petrov (GRC lead)
- Evidence packaging / report release: Daniel Carter (Compliance evidence reviewer)

3) Security technical details (encryption, logging, vuln mgmt, IR)
- Primary: Marcus Lin (Security technical reviewer)
- Controls SME: Kevin Osei / Hanae Suzuki (as needed)

4) Contractual terms (DPA, breach notification clause, liability, SLAs) / procurement redlines
- Primary: Michael Grant (Legal)
- Commercial terms / packaging commitments: Sofia Mendes (Commercial terms)

5) Urgent deadlines (same-day turnaround) for strategic deals
- Follow CS/security review escalation playbook; if truly urgent and evidence-related, escalate via GRC queue and notify Dr. Aisha Rahman only if:
  - customer exec escalation, or
  - deadline risk + NDA complete + artifacts ready, but internal bottleneck remains

Service-level expectations (set customer expectations)
- Standard questionnaire turnarounds depend on scope and whether evidence is requested.
- Evidence artifacts (SOC 2 report/policies) require NDA verification and may take longer. Don’t promise “same day” without confirming with GRC.

“Red flags” that require immediate escalation (do not answer ad hoc)
- Requests for:
  - HIPAA/BAA commitments
  - guaranteed 0-day retention across all telemetry/logging
  - specific pen test frequency/scope disclosures
  - physical security / data center audits
  - custom security addendum language requiring signature
- Any request to access or share restricted evidence folder content.

Suggested agenda for a customer security review call (30–45 min)
1) Deployment mode confirmation + data flow (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
2) Data handling: retention/deletion, data use, support access
3) Identity/access: SSO/RBAC, SCIM (if needed)
4) Logging/monitoring: audit logs + export
5) Compliance posture: SOC 2 process, evidence request steps
6) Open items + owners + due dates

Internal checklist before sending security materials
- Confirm deployment mode.
- Pull latest version from Confluence (do not use an old PDF from email).
- If sending SOC 2 evidence steps, include NDA requirement and due date request.
- Capture in CRM: which artifacts sent + version/date + next steps.

Open questions / feedback loop
- If you see new recurring questions in the field:
  - add them to the intake doc (or post in #sales with deal context)
  - include what the customer is asking for, their industry, and whether it’s Hosted/Dedicated/Private
  - do not propose new language to the customer; propose it internally for review

Owner + maintenance
- Owner for rollout/training: Stephanie Nguyen
- Program mgmt: Talia Benson
- Content approvals: Security/GRC + Product Security PM + Legal (for contractual language)

Last note (the one sentence to remember)
- If it will be pasted into an RFP or questionnaire, it must come from the approved kit language, with a version/date, and any deviations must be explicitly approved.
